group_assessment.weighting: A registry-based cohort (Dutch TSC Registry, retrospective, plus the prospective EPISTOP cohort) of 80 vigabatrin-treated TSC infants, 23 untreated TSC infants and 29 non-TSC epilepsy controls, with blinded MRI review and pre-treatment scans for every treated child. It is the better-controlled of the two VABAM cohorts read in this wave, but its population is TSC (an mTORopathy), and hormonal therapy was used in only 8 children. No WWOX patient.

entries.proposition: The cohort comprises 80 vigabatrin-treated TSC infants, 23 untreated TSC infants and 29 non-TSC epilepsy controls.
entries.snippet: We included 80 TSC infants with VGB treatment during MRI (TSC+VGB+), 23 TSC infants without VGB treatment during the entire study period (TSC+VGB−), and 29 epilepsy patients without TSC and VGB treatment (TSC−VGB−).

entries.proposition: MRI review was independent and blinded to vigabatrin status.
entries.snippet: independently reviewed by two researchers (M.L. and C.S.) blinded for VGB status

entries.proposition: VABAM-like abnormalities also occurred without vigabatrin, in 7 of 52 untreated children.
entries.snippet: Prevalence of “VABAM‐like MRI abnormalities not VGB‐related” was, therefore, 13.5% (7/52 patients).

entries.proposition: Vigabatrin was independently associated with VABAM; TSC diagnosis and refractory epilepsy were not.
entries.snippet: VGB was significantly and independently associated with the detection of VABAM (RR = 3.57, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.43–6.39), whereas refractory epilepsy (RR = .92, 95% CI = .43–1.81) and TSC (RR = .49, 95% CI = .07–1.99) were not.

entries.proposition: Concomitant hormonal or steroid therapy was not associated with the occurrence of VABAM on MRI (univariable RR 0.94).
Hormonal or steroid therapy was associated with the clinical symptoms (RR 9.00), in only eight treated patients.
entries.snippet: Concomitant hormonal or steroid therapy appeared to be a significant predictor of predefined clinical symptoms, associated with a nine times higher risk for these symptoms compared to patients without hormonal or steroid treatment (RR = 9.00, 95% CI = 2.21–18.43), although there were only eight patients treated with hormonal or steroid therapy.

entries.proposition: Hormone-treated patients had more symptoms but not higher VABAM severity scores or more regions affected.
entries.snippet: they did not have higher VABAM severity scores (p = .06, Cohen d = 1.37) or higher numbers of ROIs affected in comparison to patients without hormonal or steroid therapy (p = .77, Cohen d = −.14)

entries.proposition: VABAM was not significantly associated with the predefined clinical symptoms.
entries.snippet: The presence of VABAM (or VABAM‐like MRI abnormalities) was not significantly associated with predefined clinical symptoms (RR = 2.76, 95% CI = .68–8.77).

entries.proposition: All 13 treated children with a post-treatment MRI had complete resolution after discontinuation.
entries.snippet: In all 13 VGB‐treated patients with “VABAM possibly VGB‐related” for whom posttreatment MRIs were available, VABAM entirely resolved after VGB discontinuation

entries.proposition: The authors list a retrospective design, TSC-only treated group, and low symptom prevalence as limits; no non-TSC vigabatrin-treated group was available.
entries.snippet: First, we were not able to include a group of non‐TSC epilepsy patients with VGB treatment
